about: The questions people ask first, each with a short answer and where to go next.

rows.title: How do I install NuclearLang?
rows.summary: One command installs the release of your system: `curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh` on Linux and macOS, `irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows. At its end, with no question, it sets up the Smart Graph, the MCP server and Nuclear Chat (the profile `remote`); the AI work is done by the agents and API providers you choose (the local models are on standby).
body: ```sh
curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh        # Linux and macOS
irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows (PowerShell)
It brings `nuclear`, the language server and `nuclear-builder`, with the dialects and type definitions, into your user folders. No Rust needed.

From the source tree: `installer/install.sh` builds and installs everything and the VS Code and Zed extensions (it needs Rust; `--no-vscode`, `--no-zed`, `--uninstall`). `./install.sh --ai` then runs the set-up of the AI services over the tree's own folders.
Then check the machine: `nuclear doctor` says what is missing. For mobile apps, `nuclear setup` installs Flutter step by step.

rows.title: How do I start a project?
rows.summary: `nuclear new <name> -p backend` (or `-p mobile`, `-p web`) makes a project of `.nuc` files; `-d` picks a dialect. Then `nuclear build`, `nuclear install`, `nuclear run` and `nuclear test`.
body: ```sh
nuclear new tasks_api -p backend            # a backend (fastapi; -d nestjs for TypeScript)
nuclear new tasks_app                       # a mobile app (flutter)
nuclear new site -p web                     # a web app (react)
cd tasks_api
nuclear build && nuclear install          # transpile, then the runtime and the packages
nuclear test                                # the tests written in Nuclear
nuclear run                                 # the server, or the app on a device

Then add what the product needs, generators first: `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name> --fields "id:int name:string"` writes a whole resource; `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` writes one file of a kind. `nuclear check .` (or `nuclear check`) reports every error.
For an AI agent working in the project: `nuclear agent init` writes its `AGENTS.md` and the check hook.

rows.title: How do I run a project?
rows.summary: `nuclear run` in the project's folder builds it, installs its packages the first time and starts it: a backend's server, a web app's dev server, a mobile app on a device. In VS Code or Cursor, the Nuclear workspace (`Ctrl+Alt+N`) has the project's buttons under its name (▷ Run or Serve, ◉ Debug, ✓ Test, ⚒ Build, ☑ Check), and a backend has its scripts in the explorer's Nuclear Scripts view and in Run Task.
body: ```sh
cd tasks_api
nuclear check                               # the errors of the .nuc files, if any
nuclear run                                 # build, install the first time, then serve (Ctrl+C stops it)

- A backend answers at its URL (fastapi: `http://localhost:8000`, its API at `/docs`); saving a `.nuc` rebuilds and the server reloads. A project that uses the `ollama` plugin needs Ollama running with a model pulled.

- In the editor: `Ctrl+Alt+N` opens the Nuclear workspace; select the project's tab (`Ctrl+Alt+O` opens one) and use the buttons under its name: ▷ Serve (`Ctrl+Alt+R`, a terminal with `nuclear run`), ◉ Debug (`Ctrl+Alt+G`, breakpoints in the `.nuc`), ✓ Test, ⚒ Build, ☑ Check, and ⇄ API for a backend. Cursor hides an extension's buttons in the editor title bar: the workspace's are always there.

- A backend's scripts, like npm's: the explorer's **Nuclear Scripts** view has a ▷ for run, test, build, check, install (and migrate once there is a `migrations/` folder); *Terminal → Run Task…* lists them as `nuclear: <project>: <script>`, before the first build too.
- No play and no tasks usually means the project does not build: `nuclear check` names the errors. Run and Debug build a never-built project first and say why it fails.

rows.title: Which local models does NuclearLang use? None: they are on standby
rows.summary: None: NuclearLang's own local models (Ollama, the Nuclear Developer, the profiles `lite`, `medium`, `hard`, the local chat model) are on standby behind one switch (`localModels: false`, ADR-platform-0013). The set-up installs only `remote`: the Smart Graph (its own small model, no Ollama), the MCP server and Nuclear Chat. The AI work is done by the agents and API providers you choose.
body: - **Who does the work**: an agent on your machine (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build) or an API provider with its key in the vault (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter): Nuclear Builder's team members, Nuclear Atlas and the chat.

- **Atlas and the chat** answer with the first agent whose command is installed, else an API provider with a key, else they say a provider must be chosen; the setting `nuclear.builder.chat` picks it (Claude Code by default).

- **An older installation**: an update (`nuclear update`, or the installer again) takes away the Developer's service, the models NuclearLang pulled and Ollama when NuclearLang installed it (what was there before stays), and says how many GB it freed. A team member of the old `local` kind is converted on read to an external choice, the old file kept as `.bak`, with a warning.
- **Refused while on standby**: `nuclear-builder setup --profile lite|medium|hard`; the MCP server registers no `developer_*` tool.
- **Turning them on again** is a decision of the user: the switch `localModels` of Nuclear Builder's `setup.json`.
- **Not on standby**: an app of yours still calls a model through Ollama with the `ollama` plugin (`concept:plugins`): that is a feature of the platforms.

rows.title: Is my code sent anywhere?
rows.summary: The services of NuclearLang run on your machine and listen on `127.0.0.1` only: the Smart Graph (with its own model) and Nuclear Chat. Your code leaves the machine when you choose it: the agent or API provider that does the work reads what it is given, a spec imported from Jira or GitHub, an API read for its fields, a web search, a deploy.
body: - The graph refuses web pages (any request with an `Origin` header), gives nothing without a token you allowed (`nuclear-graph connect`, `allow`), and stores its texts encrypted (AES-256-GCM, the key in your keyring).
- The internet tools (`web_read`) refuse local addresses.

- Nuclear Builder's team members, Nuclear Atlas and the chat are worked by the agents and API providers you choose; what one reads leaves the machine, as with any frontier model. The local models are on standby (ADR-platform-0013).

- What the factory spent and made (the factory's ledger of tokens, money, time and lines, `~/.config/nuclearlang/factory/ledger/`) stays on your machine; the reports read it there (`nuclear-builder metrics`).

rows.title: Where is the generated code, and can I edit it?
rows.summary:
The generated project is in `build/` (`build/app` for a mobile or web app). It is written again on every build, so it is never edited: change the `.nuc` files. To see what a piece becomes, `nuclear build --platform

` prints it.
body: - `nuclear build` (or `nuclear build .`) writes `build/`: the target's sources, its manifest with only the packages of the enabled plugins, the wiring and the tests.
- Debugging works on the `.nuc` lines: the build keeps a line map, and `nuclear explain` tells a run-time error or a test failure at its Nuclear lines.
- When something in the generated code looks wrong, it is a bug of the dialect or a value without a type in the `.nuc`: fix the source or report it; a hand edit is lost on the next build.

rows.title: How do I ask an agent to do something?
rows.summary: In VS Code open Nuclear Atlas (`Ctrl+Alt+A`): your direct message with the general agent in Nuclear Chat, answered from the project and the Smart Graph; `/task <what to do>` there is an order, run by the Builder with your team and told in the team's channel. For a whole feature write a spec (`Ctrl+Alt+P`) with its acceptance criteria.
body: - **A question** ("what does `BooksAppComponent` expose?", "how do I add a route?"): the agent answers and changes nothing.

- **An order** (`/task add a use case that lists the books of an author`): a run of the Builder with the project's team; its members tell each station as a thread of the team's channel, and its journal says what was done.

- **A feature**: a spec in the Builder (*+ New spec*, `Ctrl+Alt+P`). Name each piece with the platform's words (a model `Book`, a repository `BookRepository`, a use case `ListBooks`) and add one acceptance criterion per behaviour. For a resource of an API, add its `GET <url>` line or an example answer and the generators write it.
- **Talk to a member** in the Builder's chat: `@qa`, `@<name>`, or the team's channel (its tech lead answers).

- **Choose who answers**: the dropdown in Atlas's header picks the agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, an API model) and its model, per conversation; by default the first agent installed, else an API provider with a key (the setting `nuclear.builder.chat`), and with none it says a provider must be chosen; it works with the Builder's MCP tools, so it can read a document, write the specs and start their runs.
- **From a terminal**: `nuclear-builder run specs/<component>/<id>/spec.md` (the run's team decides who works each station).
- **From Claude Code, Codex or Cursor**: the MCP server `nuclear-mcp` (the generators, the compiler, the graph).
The agent tells you when a task is beyond it; then give it to a stronger model or split the task.

rows.title: Which languages and frameworks does NuclearLang produce?
rows.summary: TypeScript, Dart and Python as plain languages; and through Synapsis: FastAPI (Python) or NestJS (TypeScript) for a backend, Flutter (Dart) for a mobile app, React (TypeScript) for a web app.
body: | You write | Dialect | Comes out |
| the base language | `typescript`, `dart`, `python` | a program in that language |
| the backend platform | `fastapi` | a Python service |
| the backend platform | `nestjs` | a TypeScript service |
| the mobile platform | `flutter` | a Flutter app: Android, iOS, desktop, web |
| the web platform | `react` | a React web app |
Node.js with Express is postponed. A new target is a new dialect, made of data files.

rows.title: How do I learn the syntax quickly?
rows.summary:
Begin with `nuclear help start` (MCP `nuclear_start`): what Nuclear is, the rules and the atlas of every topic. Then the short sheet: `nuclear spec --brief --dialect ` (or `--platform backend|mobile|web`). For one topic, `nuclear help `; for a kind or decorator, `nuclear help --platform

`. The compiler corrects the habits of other languages with exact fixes.
body: The eleven things that differ from TypeScript, Dart or Python:
1. Blocks by indentation of 2 spaces; no braces, no semicolons.
2. The type goes after the name: `name: string`, `f(a: int) string`.
3. The last line of a function is its value; `return` only leaves early.
4. `x = 1` declares; no `const`, `let`, `var`, `final`.
5. `User("Ana")` constructs; no `new`. Named arguments use `=`: `f(name = "Ana")`.
6. `~load()` awaits; no `await`, no `async`.
7. `and`, `or`, `not`; `x in xs` for membership.
8. `if` and `match` are values, as indented blocks; inside an argument list the value is `cond ? a : b`.
9. `"Hi ${name}"` interpolates in every string; comments are `//`.
10. No imports: the names of the target's libraries are imported by themselves.
11. A field of a module always has its type: `count: int = 0`.
Then write, run `nuclear check <file> --json`, and apply what each error says (`nuclear fix` applies the exact ones).

rows.title: How do I update NuclearLang?
rows.summary: `nuclear update` installs the latest release (the installer run again: NuclearLang and the AI services with the profile `remote`, the choices of the last install kept; what an earlier install put there for the local models is taken away). In a terminal, `nuclear` also asks `Update now? [Y]es / [n]o / [l]ater` before a command when a newer release is out.
body: One key answers; no key in 15 seconds goes on (a script in a terminal is never stopped); `l` waits a day. The check runs at most once a day (curl, or wget): the first command of the day waits at most 3 seconds for it, so the first run after an install already asks, and offline the command goes on. It never asks in editors, agents, pipes, CI, `make`, npm scripts or under `sudo`. `NUCLEAR_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns the question off.
Only an installation made by the public installers is updated this way; a `nuclear` built from source is updated the way it was built. One install runs at a time.
